title: Forming the band at the Furnace Nightclub in Cleveland
summary: Jeter and Pillars start their own band at the Furnace in January 1934 with Edison, Godley, Serp Goodson, Nunu Pitts and Snub Mosley, plus singers and charity dates.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: That was the style of the cabarets back in that day. We found out that by working all night and sometimes early and late in the morning a -- that our salary would run for a week around about $20-$25, and sometimes $30.00 a week. Which wasn't too bad during that time, in the Depression. We worked there with Chester Clark's band all through the following year through the Christmas holidays. And we gave him our notice because we were offered a job -- Jeter and myself, decided to organize a band of our own and we was offered a job on 55th -- 55th Street, near Central, a place called the Furnace -- the Furnace Nightclub. And we opened at the Furnace Nightclub January the 4th or 5th, 1934.

In the band we had A. G. Godley, the drummer; we Had Harry Sweets Edison, we had -- our reed section and we sent to Utica, New York, and got a fella named Goodson. His nickname was Serp, on the piano. And we -- on the bass we had an old gentleman, much older than us, that we had known back in the Alphonso Trent days, his days was [Nunu], I can't think of his
last name now, can you think of his last name? Can you think of his last name, Charles? Well anyway, we opened. And the band was a riot --
Louis Pitts, Louis Nunu Pitts. That's right, Pitts. The bass player, his name was Louis Nunu Pitts.
When did Snub Mosley show up?

Snub Mosley joined the band about a month later. Snub Mosley played trombone. So we worked on that job and we played requests for the people, we played a lot of beautiful, sweet music, we played a little jazz, we played a wide variety of music at this particular club. And the band became a favorite around Cleveland, Ohio.

We worked hard, and rehearsed every week to try to improve the band and keep the patrons coming. We used the same style of cabaret as we did at Mammy Louise's Creole Garden. We had a singer named Rutherford, he had a rich, golden voice, baritone voice, and he could sing "Old Man River" and make you cry.

We had several great singers, that worked at this particular club. And I can remember one lady dancing, her name was Catherine, they called her Blondie. She was the wife, now, of Count Basie. We had a beautiful relationship with the owner of the club, and with all the employees there, during our tenure at the Furnace Nightclub.

We also did some charitable work. Playing at the Phyllis Wheatly Club, and the Delta Sorority, on their Founder's day. And several times we were called onto give our services free of charge, which we did. We saved our money and saved enough money to buy brand new uniforms. Back in those days they were wearing the bi-swing suit. And we had suits made and the band made a beautiful appearance.
